   "tn10": Is it free of any major regulatory or legal threat?

   "tn13": Score it on Nash's 13 categories, 0, 5 or 10 each, using the last twelve months: cash vs debt, revenue growth, operating margin, short interest, institutional ownership, revenue growing faster than expenses, 5-year return vs the S&P 500, moat, CEO, recession-proof pricing power, secular trend, culture and mission, talent. Is the total 75 or more? Give the total in the evidence.
   "tn14": Over the last five years, has revenue grown every year, operating margin expanded, free cash flow been positive and rising, and cash exceeded debt every year?

   "tn20": Has it consistently beaten earnings expectations?

   "tn24": Working back from today's price, is the growth the price implies below what the company is already delivering?

   "tn26": Using the multiple that fits (forward P/E vs peers for mature companies, hardware and banks; Rule of 40 for software; price to sales vs the industry for unprofitable growth), is it attractive, with a PEG (forward P/E ÷ EPS growth) of 1 or less?

summaries.gardner: Apple shows several Rule Breaker traits in hindsight (a top dog with a lasting brand advantage, strong price momentum and a stock often called overvalued), but today it is a mature Rule Maker rather than a pioneer of an emerging industry. Its 52-week gain of 39.1% beats the S&P 500's 17.3%, while its core smartphone market grows slowly.
summaries.buffett: Apple fits Buffett's tenets well: an understandable consumer franchise with a powerful brand, high returns on capital, more free cash flow than net income and huge buybacks that cut the diluted share count from 17.5 billion (FY2020) to 15.0 billion (FY2025). The weak point today is price: at 39 times trailing earnings there is little margin of safety.
summaries.munger: Munger would value Apple's ecosystem lock-in, brand and capital discipline, and inverting shows relatively few ways it could fail quickly. The main risks are regulation of the App Store, the possible loss of Google's search payments, China exposure and a lag in generative AI, and paying 39 times earnings is a steep price even for a great business.
summaries.lynch: Apple is a Lynch stalwart with a simple story everyone understands (iPhone plus services), and it shrinks its share count every year. It fails his price test, though: a P/E of 39.2 against EPS growth in the low teens gives a PEG of about 3.3, and the stock is anything but overlooked.
summaries.fisher: Apple fits many of Fisher's points: a strong sales organisation and brand, a new-product pipeline (Apple silicon, Watch, AirPods, Vision Pro), high margins and loyal customers. Fisher might question whether R&D is producing big new categories now that the car project was cancelled and Apple trails in generative AI, and a new CEO took over in September 2026.
summaries.graham: Apple passes Graham's size, ten-year profitability and EPS growth tests (diluted EPS rose from $2.31 in FY2015 to $7.46 in FY2025). It fails on dividend history (resumed only in 2012) and on price: a P/E of 39.2 and P/B of 46.4 are far above his limits.
summaries.thiel: Apple has strong answers on distribution, durability and engineering, with a vertically integrated ecosystem that is hard to copy. But it competes in large, crowded markets rather than holding a monopoly, and today it is not clearly ten times better than rivals such as Samsung or Google Pixel.
summaries.gerstner: Apple is a high-quality compounder, but on Gerstner's growth-adjusted valuation lens it looks expensive: a forward P/E of about 37 for revenue growth expected around 15% in FY2026 and lower after. It is a follower rather than a leader in the AI platform shift he emphasises.
summaries.druckenmiller: Apple's results have strengthened (June-quarter 2026 revenue +16% to a record $109.4B) and the stock is up 39% in a year, which fits Druckenmiller's interest in momentum and improving fundamentals. The price already exceeds the average analyst target of $329, so there is less obvious upside surprise ahead.
summaries.smith: Apple meets Smith's 'good company' criteria: very high returns on capital, strong free cash flow (TTM $136.7B), a dominant brand and recurring services revenue. It fails his 'don't overpay' test at a free-cash-flow yield of about 2.7% and a P/E near 39.
summaries.greenblatt: Apple ranks very well on Greenblatt's return-on-capital measure (ROIC about 102%), but its earnings yield is low: EV/EBIT of 31.8 is about 3.1%. It would not rank highly on the combined Magic Formula today.
summaries.akre: Apple has an extraordinary business and a capable management team, two legs of Akre's stool. The reinvestment leg is weak, because Apple returns most of its cash through buybacks and dividends rather than reinvesting it at high returns.
summaries.pabrai: Pabrai has praised capital-light, buyback-heavy compounders, but Apple at 39 times earnings is not the cheap, distressed, low-risk bet that 'The Dhandho Investor' describes. There is no temporary setback depressing the price now.
summaries.wood: Apple is not one of ARK's core disruptive-innovation names; it leads in custom chips and wearables but trails in AI and has no major position in robotics, energy storage, blockchain or genomic sequencing. Its markets are large but mature, so it fits Wood's framework poorly.
summaries.ackman: Apple fits much of Ackman's checklist: simple, predictable, free-cash-flow generative, with a dominant brand and high barriers to entry. Less fitting are its exposure to China and tariffs and a price that leaves little room for an attractive return.
summaries.sleep: Apple has a scale-driven ecosystem with growing switching costs, but it keeps its scale benefits as high margins and premium prices rather than passing them back to customers in the way Sleep's 'scale economics shared' model admires (e.g. Costco, Amazon).
summaries.valentine: Apple was itself a Sequoia investment of Don Valentine in 1978 and fits his focus on huge markets and great products. Today it is a mature giant rather than the kind of early-stage, market-creating company Valentine sought.
summaries.nash: Apple passes many of Tom Nash's quality tests: revenue grew 14% in the last twelve months, operating margin is 33%, free cash flow is huge and steady, and it beat estimates in each of the last four quarters, scoring about 105 of 130 on his 13 categories. It fails his valuation steps, with a forward P/E of 37, a PEG of 3.3 and a DCF value well below the $341 price, and it is not built for a new secular trend. Debt exceeds cash and short-term investments unless long-term securities are counted, the current ratio is only 1.0, and a new CEO took over in September 2026.

momentum.evidence: AAPL closed at $341.27 on 13 October 2026, up 39.1% over 52 weeks, versus a 17.3% price gain for the S&P 500 over the year to 13 October 2026.

g4.evidence: Apple is led by long-time Apple executives (CEO John Ternus since September 2026, with Tim Cook as executive chairman), and has long been one of Berkshire Hathaway's largest holdings.

g6.evidence: The price of $341.27 is above the average analyst target of $329.38, and many commentators call a P/E of 39 too high for a company growing in the low teens.

simple.evidence: Apple sells iPhones, Macs, iPads, wearables and services that most people use, a business a careful generalist can understand.

b2.evidence: Revenue rose from $274.5B (FY2020) to $416.2B (FY2025), falling only in FY2023 (-2.8%), and it has stayed highly profitable for many years.

integrity.evidence: Apple has a single share class, a strong governance record, clear reporting, and it has returned most of its cash through buybacks and dividends; executive pay is tied to relative shareholder return.

b6.evidence: Apple avoids large acquisitions and builds its own chips and products, and it cancelled the car project in 2024 rather than chase it.

roic.evidence: ROIC is about 102% (StockAnalysis, October 2026); it carries $84.3B of debt but held $146.5B of cash and marketable securities in June 2026, so returns do not depend on leverage.

fcf.evidence: Trailing free cash flow was $136.7B against net income of $128.9B to June 2026, so it turns more than all of its profit into cash.

b10.evidence: Apple pays out more than it earns through buybacks, and its market value has grown to about $5.0 trillion, far more than the earnings it has kept.

safety.evidence: At 39.2 times trailing earnings and above the average analyst target, the price is not below a conservative estimate of value.

fairprice.evidence: A forward P/E of 37.0 and a PEG of 3.3 are high for expected EPS growth of only about 6% next year based on forward versus trailing earnings.

mu5.evidence: With over 2 billion active devices, a net cash position and strong switching costs, the main threats (regulation, loss of Google search payments, China, AI) could dent but are unlikely to break the business.

reinvest.evidence: Apple cannot reinvest most of its profits internally and returns them instead; the diluted share count fell from 17.5 billion (FY2020) to 15.0 billion (FY2025).

ly2.evidence: Apple is a stalwart: a giant, steadily growing company whose story is selling premium devices to a loyal base and growing services revenue.

ly3.evidence: Its P/E of 39.2 is far above its earnings growth rate (EPS rose from $6.08 in FY2024 to $7.46 in FY2025), and the PEG is about 3.3.

runway.evidence: Services, wearables, India and new categories can add growth, but iPhone, about half of sales, is in a mature market.

ly7.evidence: The share count fell 2.1% over the past year through buybacks, but insiders own only about 0.06% and mostly sell stock awards rather than buy.

ly8.evidence: Apple is one of the most widely owned and followed stocks, with 44 analysts covering it.

fi2.evidence: Apple has kept adding products as older ones matured, such as Apple Watch, AirPods, Apple silicon Macs, its own C1 modem and Vision Pro.

fi3.evidence: R&D produced industry-leading A-series and M-series chips, but some large bets such as the car project (cancelled 2024) and the delayed Siri AI revamp have not paid off.

fi4.evidence: Apple's marketing, retail stores and carrier partnerships are among the best in the world, letting it charge premium prices for a 19.7% share of 2025 smartphone shipments.

longterm.evidence: Apple spent many years developing its own chips and modem and invests in privacy and long product cycles, even at some short-term cost.

gr1.evidence: Apple had $416.2B of FY2025 revenue and a market capitalization of about $5.0 trillion.

ni10.evidence: Apple has been profitable every year for well over ten years, with net income of $112.0B in FY2025.

gr4.evidence: Apple resumed paying dividends only in 2012 after a 17-year gap, so it lacks an unbroken 20-year record.

eps10.evidence: Diluted EPS rose from $2.31 (split-adjusted) in FY2015 to $7.46 in FY2025, more than tripling.

gr6.evidence: The trailing P/E is 39.2, more than double Graham's limit of about 15.

gr7.evidence: P/E of 39.2 times P/B of 46.4 is about 1,815, far above Graham's 22.5 ceiling.

th1.evidence: Apple's products are excellent and its chips lead on efficiency, but rivals such as Samsung and Google Pixel are close substitutes rather than ten times worse.

timing.evidence: An AI-driven upgrade cycle helped June-quarter 2026 revenue rise 16%, but Apple is a follower in generative AI and relies partly on Google Gemini.

th3.evidence: Apple started with a big share of the small personal-computer market in the late 1970s and later expanded via iPod and iPhone, but it never dominated PCs.

team.evidence: Apple has deep, experienced management, but new CEO John Ternus took over only on 1 September 2026 and is not yet proven in the top job.

th5.evidence: Apple controls its distribution through more than 500 retail stores, its online store, the App Store and carrier partners worldwide.

durable.evidence: Its brand, ecosystem and over 2 billion active devices have strengthened over two decades and are likely to remain hard to dislodge, though AI devices are a long-term risk.

th7.evidence: Apple's integrated hardware-software model was once a unique insight, but today its opportunities are well understood by everyone.

trend.evidence: Apple benefits from on-device AI driving upgrades, but it is not a leading beneficiary of the AI platform shift like chip and cloud companies.

dr1.evidence: Revenue growth sped up to 16% in the June 2026 quarter and FY2026 consensus is about +15%, but forward EPS is only about 6% above trailing EPS.

dr2.evidence: Services growth and an AI upgrade cycle may help, but these are widely expected and Apple faces App Store and search-payment regulatory risk.

dr4.evidence: Apple has net cash so rates matter little to its finances, but consumer spending, tariffs and the US-China relationship affect demand and costs.

dr6.evidence: Catalysts include FY2026 fourth-quarter results due in late October 2026, the revamped Siri and new product categories under the new CEO.

dr7.evidence: Apple's quality supports a large position for many investors, but its high valuation and slower growth limit conviction for a concentrated bet.

gm.evidence: Trailing gross margin is 48.7%, very high for a hardware maker, and services margins are much higher.

fcfyield.evidence: The free-cash-flow yield is about 2.7% ($136.7B trailing FCF on a $5.0 trillion market cap), modest for revenue growth expected to slow after FY2026.

gb2.evidence: EV/EBIT is 31.8, an earnings yield of about 3.1%, which is low by Magic Formula standards.

pa2.evidence: Apple is not in a setback; it reported record June-quarter revenue and the stock is near record highs.

pa4.evidence: The business is very resilient, but at 39 times earnings a de-rating could cause a large loss in the share price.

wo1.evidence: Apple leads in AI-capable consumer chips but is not a leader in generative AI models, robotics, energy storage, blockchain or sequencing.

wo2.evidence: Apple's product costs and prices are not falling rapidly; it raises prices and holds premium margins.

wo3.evidence: It combines custom chips, on-device AI, health sensing and spatial computing, but none is yet a major new growth platform.

wo4.evidence: Its main markets (smartphones, PCs, tablets, wearables) are large and mature and are unlikely to be many times larger in five years.

ac3.evidence: Apple is little affected by commodity prices or rates, but tariffs, China manufacturing and consumer spending affect it.

ns1.evidence: Apple keeps the benefits of its scale as premium prices and margins rather than passing them back to customers.

ns4.evidence: Its installed base and services should keep growing, but AI-first devices and regulation make it unclear it will be clearly stronger in 10-20 years.

va2.evidence: Apple's devices solve everyday needs for communication and computing well, but their value is more convenience and quality than relief of a painful, unsolved problem.

tn1.evidence: Apple is a consumer-device and services company adding on-device AI to existing products rather than a company built for the AI, energy or robotics infrastructure trend.

tn2.evidence: The market already sees Apple as a premium devices-plus-services ecosystem, which is what it is; there is no clear hidden transformation the market misses.

tn3.evidence: Apple is a $5.0 trillion US mega-cap, not a small cap, Chinese company, commodity producer, airline or startup, though its December quarter is seasonally the largest.

tn4.evidence: It passes all three if long-term securities are counted: revenue grew in FY2024, FY2025 and the last twelve months, it earned $128.9B of trailing net income, and cash and marketable securities of $146.5B exceed $84.3B of debt (June 2026).

tn5.evidence: Free cash flow was positive in each of the last six quarters (from $20.9B to $51.6B), and cash plus marketable securities exceeded total debt each quarter, though cash and short-term investments alone were below debt.

tn6.evidence: Trailing-twelve-month revenue to June 2026 was $466.8B, up about 14.2% from $408.6B a year earlier.

tn7.evidence: Revenue growth of about 14.2% plus a free-cash-flow margin of about 29.3% ($136.7B on $466.8B) gives about 43.5, just above 40.

tn8.evidence: Over the last twelve months revenue grew 14.2% while total costs including cost of sales grew about 12.1%, but R&D plus SG&A grew faster, about 19.4%.

tn9.evidence: It passes on market cap, short interest (0.8%), operating margin (33%), revenue growth (14%), earnings beats and age, but cash and short-term investments of $62.4B are below debt of $84.3B unless $84.1B of long-term securities are counted.

tn10.evidence: Apple faces major legal threats: the US Justice Department antitrust suit filed in 2024, EU Digital Markets Act rulings on the App Store, and remedies in the Google search case that affect its roughly $20B of annual search payments.

tn11.evidence: Apple provides iPhones, Macs and services that help consumers communicate, work and play in one secure, easy ecosystem, and charges premium hardware prices plus subscriptions and App Store commissions; people choose it for design, privacy and how well its devices work together.

tn13.evidence: Scoring 5 for cash vs debt, 5 for revenue growth (14%), 10 for operating margin (33%), short interest (0.8%) and institutional ownership (66%), 5 for revenue vs expenses, 10 for 5-year return (roughly +140% vs about +80% for the S&P 500), moat, pricing power, culture and talent, and 5 each for its new CEO and secular trend gives about 105 of 130.

tn14.evidence: Revenue fell 2.8% in FY2023 and free cash flow has not risen steadily, even though operating margin has edged up and cash plus securities have exceeded debt.

tn15.evidence: Interest costs are tiny and liabilities are 2.6 times equity and the current ratio is 1.00, but total assets of $383.3B are only 1.4 times liabilities of $275.7B, short of 2x (June 2026).

tn18.evidence: John Ternus became CEO only on 1 September 2026, so he has no track record in the role or 10+ years as CEO, and insiders own about 0.06% with no open-market buying.

tn20.evidence: Apple beat consensus EPS and revenue in each of the last four quarters, e.g. $2.02 vs $1.89 EPS and $109.4B vs $108.9B revenue in the June 2026 quarter.

tn21.evidence: There is no clown CEO, co-CEO, acquisition spree, accounting concern or auditor change; margins are rising and the CEO handover from Tim Cook to John Ternus was orderly.

tn22.evidence: Apple has $466.8B of revenue, $136.7B of free cash flow and a shrinking share count, the opposite of a hype stock.

tn24.evidence: At about 37 times free cash flow the price implies roughly 10% or more annual FCF growth for a decade, above Apple's 8.7% average revenue growth from FY2020 to FY2025.

tn25.evidence: Using a 3-year average revenue growth of about 2% (or even 10%), an FCF margin of about 28%, 4% terminal growth and a 12% discount rate gives roughly $110-150 per share, far below the $341 price.

tn26.evidence: A forward P/E of 37 is high for a mature hardware company and the PEG is about 3.3, well above 1.
